extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; policymakers and general readers interested in classical economics
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of classical political‑economy principles relating wages, labour demand, population growth, and the real standard of living; argumentative prose illustrating causes and effects across countries and historical circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population growth as the decisive mark of prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: The most decisive mark of the prosperity of any country is the increase of the number of its inhabitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith contrasts Great Britain (very slow doubling) with British North America (doubling in 20–25 years), noting that rapid multiplication of inhabitants signals thriving and advancing acquisition of riches; this increase is often due to higher birth rates rather than migration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic value of children encourages marriage and fertility
rubrics_metrics.description: Where labour is well rewarded, a numerous family is a source of opulence; the labour of each child contributes materially to family income and thus encourages early marriage and high fertility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in North America a child's labour before leaving home is 'computed to be worth a hundred pounds' to parents; a widow with children can be economically attractive in marriage markets. 'The value of children is the greatest of all encouragements to marriage.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Stationary national wealth tends to depress wages
rubrics_metrics.description: Even a very wealthy country, if long stationary in wealth, will typically have low wages because the existing funds of revenue and stock can easily supply a stable demand for labour without scarcity of hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When funds and demand remain constant across centuries, labour supply may exceed employment causing constant scarcity of employment and wages reducing to the lowest humane rate; China is offered as an example of a fertile, populous, industrious country that is long stationary and exhibits low wages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decaying maintenance funds lead to depopulation and misery
rubrics_metrics.description: If the funds destined for the maintenance of labour sensibly decay, demand for servants falls, unemployment rises, wages collapse, and want, famine, and mortality spread until population falls to match remaining resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith outlines a causal cascade: reduced funds → fewer employments → competition and lower wages → starvation, begging, crime → mortality and depopulation; he suggests Bengal and some East India settlements as possible cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberal reward of labour is both effect and cause of increasing national wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: High wages are a natural symptom of increasing national wealth and also act as a cause by encouraging population growth and industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith argues that liberal wages enable people to rear more children, supply rising labour demand, and increase industry: 'The liberal reward of labour, therefore, as it is the necessary effect, so it is the natural symptom of increasing national wealth.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Wages are not simply regulated by subsistence needs or price of provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Wages do not consistently fluctuate with the price of provisions nor are they always set at the minimal subsistence level required for family maintenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith gives four empirical points: (1) seasonal differences (summer wages higher despite lower fuel costs), (2) wages often do not rise with higher food prices and can remain stable for decades, (3) wages vary more by place than provisions prices (e.g., higher in towns than nearby countryside), and (4) wages' spatial/time variations can be opposite to provisions' price variations (e.g., grain dearer in Scotland but wages lower).

rubrics_metrics.name: Real recompense matters more than nominal wages
rubrics_metrics.description: The real quantity of necessaries and conveniences labour can procure (real recompense) has often increased even faster than the money price of labour because many goods have become cheaper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include cheaper potatoes, turnips, garden produce, and improvements in coarse linen and woollen manufactures that provide cheaper clothing and tools; taxes on soap, salt, candles have raised some prices but do not offset widespread reductions in other goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand for labour regulates population growth (market mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The demand for labour operates like demand for any commodity: it regulates the production of men — increasing demand quickens propagation, and excessive supply or deficiency corrects itself by raising or lowering wages and thus population growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith explains an automatic market feedback: if wages are less than needed for replacement, deficiency raises wages; if wages are more, over-multiplication lowers wages — driving population toward what labour demand requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free labour is, in the long run, cheaper and better managed than slave labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the wear and tear of a slave is said to be at the master's expense, in practice free servants manage their own maintenance frugally and thereby often cost less over time than slaves managed negligently by owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith attributes this to differences in management: the poor's strict frugality vs. the negligent master/overseer; empirical observations even in Boston, New York, and Philadelphia show freemen's work cheaper in the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Piece-work can produce excessive application and occupational ill-health
rubrics_metrics.description: When workmen are liberally paid by the piece they are apt to overwork themselves and ruin their health and constitution in a few years; moderation often preserves health and long-run productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith notes examples (carpenters lasting only ~8 years in full vigour), military examples where officers limited soldiers' daily earnings, and cites Ramazzini on trade-specific diseases. He argues moderate, sustainable work often yields the greatest annual output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheap years and dear years differently affect labour supply and hiring
rubrics_metrics.description: In years of plenty (cheap provisions), servants often leave masters to work independently and farmers hire more labour; in years of scarcity (dear provisions), masters employ fewer servants and many independent workmen return to wage labour, depressing wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cheap years increase the fund for maintenance and thus demand for servants; dear years reduce such funds and force independent workers into service or accept lower wages, benefiting masters who find more humble labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative immobility of labour keeps local wage differentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite price differentials that would seem to motivate migration, people are hard to transport; significant wage differences between neighboring parishes and regions persist because labour does not move easily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith observes wages can be 20–25% higher in a town than nearby countryside and that, unlike goods, people are 'the most difficult' to transport — so disparities persist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poverty lowers child survival even if fertility is high
rubrics_metrics.description: While poverty may not prevent high fertility, it severely reduces the survival and rearing of children; high births among the poor are offset by high child mortality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Highland mothers bearing many children with few surviving; high mortality among children of common people, foundling hospitals, and parish charities; poverty produces higher mortality before ages four, seven, or ten.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate industriousness of poor depends on material circumstances, not moralizing claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that cheap years make the poor lazier and dear years more industrious is overstated; overall industry tends to be greater when people are in better health and spirits, not when they are ill-fed or demoralized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith argues years of dearth bring sickness and mortality reducing productivity; empirical manufacturing accounts (e.g., Elbeuf, Rouen registers) show mixed relationships and that stationary manufactures don't reliably produce more work in dear years.
